title: Travel English Shadowing: 40 Useful Sentences for Airports, Hotels, Restaurants and Getting Help

segments.text: Have you ever walked up to a hotel desk in another country and suddenly forgotten every English word you know? You understand the question, but your answer just won't come out.
That feeling is more common than you think, and the solution is practice that feels like real life.
Hello everyone, and welcome back to English Fluency Teacher. Today we're going to practice useful travel English through shadowing.
The lesson has four parts. We'll practice English for the airport, for hotels, for restaurants, and for asking for help and directions.
Before each part, I'll briefly explain when you can use that English. Then we'll begin the shadowing practice.
I'll say each sentence two times. After each time, repeat it aloud. Don't only copy the words. Try to copy the tone, the rhythm, and the friendly, confident way the sentence is spoken.
Don't worry about mistakes. Just keep going. Ready?
Let's begin.
Warm-Up: Travel Mindset
I can use simple English to travel with confidence.
I don't need perfect grammar to ask for help.
Every sentence I practice makes my next trip easier.
Part 1: At the Airport
Airports are busy, and staff often speak quickly. The goal here is to ask short, clear questions, check important details, and ask for help politely when something goes wrong.
Now, let's shadow these sentences.
Excuse me, where is the check-in desk for this flight?
I'd like to check in, please. Here is my passport.
Could I have a window seat, if one is available?
I have one bag to check and one to carry on.
Is my flight still leaving on time?
Which gate should I go to, please?
What time does boarding start?
Sorry, I think I'm in the wrong line. Could you help me?
Excuse me, my bag hasn't arrived yet. Who should I speak to?
Thank you for your help. Have a great day.
Part 2: At the Hotel
Excellent. Now let's move to the hotel. Here you'll need to check in, ask about services, and politely report small problems without sounding angry.
Notice how many of these sentences begin with, could you, or, would it be possible. That small change makes a request sound friendly instead of demanding.
Hello, I have a reservation under my name.
I'd like to check in, please. I booked a room for three nights.
Could you tell me what time breakfast is served?
Would it be possible to have a late check-out?
The air conditioning in my room isn't working. Could someone take a look?
Could I get some extra towels, please?
What's the Wi-Fi password, please?
Would it be possible to change to a quieter room?
Could you call a taxi for me at eight tomorrow morning?
segments.spoken: Could you call a taxi for me at eight tomorrow morning?

segments.text: Thank you. The room is perfect.
Part 3: At a Restaurant
Great work. Now let's practice restaurant English. Compare these two sentences. Give me the bill. And, could we get the bill, please?
Both sentences ask for the same thing, but the second one sounds warmer and more natural. In this part, you'll practice ordering, asking about food, solving small problems, and paying politely.
A table for two, please. Do you have anything available now?
Could we see the menu, please?
What would you recommend for someone who likes mild food?
I'd like the chicken salad and a glass of water, please.
Does this dish have any meat in it? I'm vegetarian.
Could I have the sauce on the side?
Excuse me, I think there's a mistake with my order.
Could we get the bill, please?
Is service included, or should I leave a tip?
Everything was delicious. Thank you very much.
Part 4: Asking for Help and Directions
segments.spoken: Part four. Asking for help and directions.

segments.text: Great job. For our final part, we'll practice something every traveler needs. Asking for help when you're lost, confused, or in a hurry.
These sentences will help you ask people to slow down, repeat, or show you the way. Let's finish strongly.
Excuse me, could you tell me how to get to the train station?
Is it far from here, or can I walk?
Sorry, could you speak a little more slowly, please?
Could you write that down for me?
I think I'm lost. Could you show me where we are on the map?
Which bus goes to the city center?
How much is a ticket to the airport?
Where can I buy a SIM card around here?
I've lost my wallet. Where is the nearest police station?
Thank you so much. You've been really kind.
Excellent work. You've just practiced 40 useful travel sentences across four real situations.
But the goal wasn't only to memorize phrases. You practiced how to check in, make polite requests, order food, solve small problems, and ask for help when you need it.
If you completed the full practice, write in the comments, I'm ready to travel in English. And tell me which situation you'd like to practice next.
When you watch this lesson again, listen to the tone as well as the words. Keep practicing, keep shadowing, and most importantly, keep speaking English.
